claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion arises from atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements.
Lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
The proposed initial material is a random solid-solution HEA containing at least five principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions.
Substituting elements with elements of different atomic radii while preserving equiatomic proportions can systematically vary atomic-size mismatch.
Identical processing can be used to obtain sufficiently comparable microstructures for the mechanical comparison.
The root-mean-square atomic-size difference δ quantifies lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch produces greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength.
Hardness and strength will increase as δ increases relative to a low-δ baseline alloy.
An HEA composed of elements with similar atomic radii provides a low-δ baseline.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for random solid-solution HEAs without significant secondary phases or ordering.
Electronic and magnetic effects may also contribute to hardness and strength.
Processing conditions may affect microstructure and thereby influence the measured mechanical properties.
Lattice distortion represented as δ can be measured using X-ray diffraction or another suitable technique.
A failure of hardness and strength to increase consistently with δ, or a decrease despite increasing δ, would falsify the hypothesis.
